utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis. We are assisted today by our intern, Jaspreet Saini, and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to greet everybody in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and everybody else in the courtroom. We have to continue hearing the witness. Before that, Mr. Mundis has to finish his cross-examination this morning. So you should finish before 12.30, which is going to allow the Defence to re-examine the witness in the afternoon. And if everything goes well, the Judges will also have the time on Thursday morning to ask their questions. And we will also have the afternoon for the questions by both parties. That is the plan until Friday. This is more or less how we are going to proceed. We are going to have the witness escorted into the courtroom, and we'll have the translation. Mr. Mundis, can you assure us that you will finish this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. And I at this point don't anticipate going as long as 12.30, although I'm partially beheld to the witness in terms of the length of the answers to the questions that I put to him. But I would not anticipate going until 12.30. I would anticipate finishing slightly before that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. I hope that you had a good rest because today's going to be a long day, as you know. We have this hearing this morning, and then we continue after -- in the afternoon. We are going to have a lunch break between 12.30 and 2.00. This will allow everybody to have some rest, and then we will resume in the afternoon. I believe that we have received a translation. Does everybody have the translation? I don't know whether the French translation comes directly from B/C/S or whether it went via English. The document doesn't show it. In any case, the English translation we have. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could start by, again, providing the witness with the bundle of documents that the Prosecution had prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you could please return to the exhibit marked P429. And again, sir, if you could look to the section that we were talking about yesterday under the subheading "proposal." Have you found that portion of the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you'd look at the third sentence under "proposal" where it says "engagement of foreign nationals," can you please tell us, first of all, what that phrase means to you or to the people who were discussing this. What exactly were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this sentence, I can see and I interpret this as follows: The question is raised as to whether they will continue being engaged, but not whether we will engage them. They are engaged. Now, as to who engages them, we don't know. That's why the question is put here whether they will still be engaged, whether they will continue being engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: The document that we have in front of us represents, in effect, the minutes of this meeting held on the 23rd of June 1993. And I would like to focus your attention not on the minutes, but on the actual discussions. Do you remember what was discussed at that meeting concerning this issue of engagement? Can you add anything that's not reflected in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the entire minutes, so I could not check what else is there. You are -- you keep channeling my attention on this proposal, especially on one part of those proposals. I can't answer your question because I haven't read the minutes in -- thoroughly. It's very hard for me to remember what was being said at that meeting. I would have to think long and hard who said what at that meeting in order for me to be able to remember those words after 11 and a half years. It's very difficult for me, therefore, to answer your question and to say what was being said at the meeting. If I were to read what it says in the minutes, I would be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we're clear then, at this point you don't have any recollection of what was said at the meeting concerning the issue of the engagement of foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember some things; however, I can't remember all the details of that meeting. I remember that at the meeting, amongst other things, the problem of foreigners was raised, and problems we had with foreigners. The -- at that meeting, the corps commander informed us what had already been done in order to deal with the problem of foreigners and what would continue being done with that respect. I also remember the way commander said that on the 23rd of June. I've already said something about that. I have said that we sent a request to our superior command and that on the 16th of June, we received a document from the supreme command staff. By this document, it was said to us that we should transfer those foreigners to Igman or possibly disarm them. We had already discussed the topic of possible disarmament of these foreigners, but nothing was said precisely. We carried out a lot of assessment and evaluation of that in the 3rd Corps command, and we concluded that it would be very difficult to carry through because we did not have the accurate estimate of the number of these people, where they had come from, who had sent them, what their intentions were, how well trained they were. I told you what information we had. According to our information, they distributed money among people. They married girls, very young girls in our villages. We also had information that they distributed food among people. I have already spoken at great length about that, but I can go over that again if you want me to do so. At this meeting, the commander informed us what was being done, and we concluded that the problem of foreigners is rather big, that it should be solved, that we should seek the assistance of the superior command. The corps command was of the opinion that this problem could not be resolved at the level of the corps, that the superior command should be involved in order to deal with the presence of foreigners in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, a couple of questions, because you have mentioned these problems several times. And I want to ask you if your concerns were that if you were to take any action against these foreigners, the local population that was receiving food from them and/or the local women who married them, would that have posed an additional threat to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we believed that it would pose a major threat to the 3rd Corps because we did not have enough means to draw forces from the defence lines against the aggressors. Two-thirds of our troops were engaged on the lines facing the aggressor, and we thought that it would be very difficult to get involved in a showdown with these foreigners because we did not have enough information available to us. And we were of the opinion that we would eventually have to clash with our local population that had blood ties with the foreigners. I've told you that some of the local population depended on those foreigners for food because the 3rd Corps could not have provided them with food. I've already said that. And I can repeat it. This is the essence of what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any estimate as to how much dependence there was by the local population on these foreigners or how many local women had married foreigners?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has already answered that on several occasions. The fact that my learned friend keeps on insisting on that is against the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is dismissed. The Prosecution would like to know how come that the fact that these foreigners provided food to the population and the fact that they married local girls, why would that have an impact on the way the 3rd Corps handled the issue of mujahedin? The witness has to answer this type of question, especially when it comes to the military issues of that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. At that time, we did not have reliable information as to how many foreigners were married to the local girls. We did not have the exact number of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have -- did you have any kind of estimate?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have some estimates. We believed that there was a considerable number -- a significant number of girls that were married to those foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, what do you mean by "considerable" or "significant"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that we did not have the precise number, but it also means that a lot of girls were married to those foreigners. This is what I mean. Those were not just individual, few-and-far-between cases. The number was significant. If we had had precise information, we could have ended up with a more precise estimate. At that time, the 3rd Corps became aware of that problem, the problem of the presence of foreigners which might eventually jeopardise the ultimate mission of the 3rd Corps. And that was to defend the area from the aggressor. That was the mission of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, I take it that because you've told us that you weren't sure where these foreigners were within the 3rd Corps area, would that also follow that you weren't aware of where within the 3rd Corps area these foreigners were marrying local girls?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We didn't know where these girls were and where they came from, from which areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- did you have any information as to local pockets where these foreigners were marrying local women, or was it completely throughout the area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that information at that moment, at least I was not aware of the precise locations, the areas they were from. We were aware of the fact that these girls came from various areas of the zone of responsibility of the corps. So it was not a localised area within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. I would like to point out again that the time between these foreigners came and became of some interest for the 3rd Corps was really very short. During that short period of time, the services that were dealing with those matters did not have enough time to come up with precise data, with precise locations where this was happening, to come up with the precise number of girls that married them, to come up with a precise number of local population that were closely linked with the foreigners. I also told you that they were very mobile and that it was very difficult to follow them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the time between when these foreigners came and the time when they became of interest for the 3rd Corps was very short. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. They were still not important for the 3rd Corps in comparison with the main issue of the 3rd Corps. At that time, the 3rd Corps had its mission which was more important than the problem of foreigners at the time. This is what I said. I also said that before this time, in the preceding period, we did not believe that foreigners were a major issue. I told you when foreigners became a prominent issue. This was when we had learned from the European monitors that the Croatian officers had been kidnapped by foreigners, and then there was this incident in Miletici. And we saw then that this group of foreigners was rather militant. I have already spoken about that. And we're talking about the end of April, whereas this meeting here took place in the month of June. So this is the short period of time for the 3rd Corps to be aware of all the information and to come up with some precise estimate. I told you that we didn't know how many foreigners there were, how they were entering Bosnia and Herzegovina. We didn't know what their goal was, what arms they had at their disposal. We also didn't know how well they were educated and trained. I've already spoken about that. It was very difficult for us in such a short period of time when your main issue is to defend your country against aggression when, in the month of June, we already had major problems with the Croatian Defence Council. We already had two fronts. I've already spoken about that in great detail. This is what I know. This is the information that I had. It was very difficult for us in such a short period of time to come up with detailed and thorough estimate of the numbers of foreigners that would enable us to carry out radical measures. We asked our superior command to help us because we were not satisfied with the way things developed. If we had been satisfied, we would have undertaken more radical activities. However, at that moment, we could not do anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, you told us about the distribution of food by these foreigners. And again, you'll agree with me that we're using the term "foreigner" as meaning armed foreigners. How much -- what percentage or what estimate of the population was reliant upon these foreigners for food?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be similar to the answer provided to you about the girls. At that time, we did not have information as to what percentage of the population relied on foreigners for food. As for the foreigners, they were armed, and they were militant. We did not have precise information as to what percentage of population received food from those foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, again, sir, do you have any kind of estimate? Was it a very small percentage or a medium-size or a large percentage?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we couldn't -- I can't give you such a conclusion. I can't give you whether the percentage was small, medium, or high. This is all relative. And we did not have any idea of the areas where people relied more or less heavily on foreigners for food. Can you please be precise in your questions. Then I can maybe provide you with a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were the -- was the distribution of food by foreigners done in local pockets; or again, was it throughout the area of the 3rd Corps? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know anything about the exact locations. All I can say is that this occurred in several places, in several areas that the corps was responsible for. People distributed this aid on the move, in fact. I know that there were other humanitarian organisations involved in the distribution of food to the population, and they had specific locations where this food would be distributed. But in the case of these foreigners, we couldn't locate a centre and focus our attention on that centre. We couldn't say "that's where the location is, that's where these armed foreigners are distributing food to the population." So we weren't in a position to see how many people were living in such areas. We didn't have the information we needed to make a real assessment. That's the essence of the problem. One day they would distribute aid at one location, and another day at another location. We were not in a position to know who received food from them and who didn't receive food from them. We really didn't have the means of determining such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how did the foreigners distribute this food? Was it by lorries or was it out of the back of Volkswagen Golfs? Did they have camels? Were they carrying this on their back? How did they move this food throughout the 3rd Corps area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that they didn't use camels to distribute this food because if they had done so, it would have been interesting for the people in Bosnia. There were no camels in Bosnia. But I don't know whether they used lorries or horses to distribute the food. I don't know whether they carried the food themselves. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to how they got the food into Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that we wondered about, too. We had no information as to how they would receive food from abroad. We really couldn't make any assessments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us a lot about HVO checkpoints. Were there also ABiH-3rd Corps checkpoints at certain locations or throughout the 3rd Corps area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were checkpoints, but we didn't control humanitarian organisations at military checkpoints. We didn't control foreigners who passed through. We controlled members of the ABiH at those checkpoints. At the checkpoints of the ABiH, we controlled the passage of military vehicles. We didn't check civilians or humanitarian organisations to check to see what they were transporting. This was the duty of the civilian police. This was not the military police's duty. It wasn't the duty of the military police to do this at checkpoints under the control of the ABiH. So at the checkpoints, we didn't know anything about those who were bringing food and other things in. We didn't control the humanitarian organisations. We didn't control the UNPROFOR. We didn't control the European monitors. At the ABiH checkpoints, we only controlled members of the ABiH and equipment that these members had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand what you've said, sir, if these foreigners, these armed foreigners, approached an ABiH checkpoint, they would simply be waved through?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, armed foreigners didn't pass through the ABiH checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, at line 9 on page 12, you said "we didn't control foreigners who passed through," and for the past two or three days we have been using the term "foreigners" to describe armed foreigners. Did the ABiH allow armed foreigners free passage through ABiH-controlled checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, various foreigners passed through ABiH checkpoints. Other units passed through these checkpoints, too. The HVO passed through these checkpoints. They would carry arms. We wouldn't disarm the HVO. If they weren't part of the ABiH, we would not disarm them, nor would we control them. That wasn't our duty. That wasn't our mission. It wasn't our mission to control all those who were under arms. There were people there who were also providing security for their companies, and they had the right to carry arms. Then there was the reserve police force that passed through. We quite simply did not control all those who were carrying weapons. We controlled the members of the ABiH. This is what I'm trying to tell you. The 3rd Corps's duty, the 3rd Corps's task at the time was not to control all those who were carrying weapons and who passed through those ABiH checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what do you mean by "control" when we're talking about checkpoints? Are you saying that the only people who were stopped at ABiH checkpoints were members of the ABiH? And that everyone else, HVO, UNPROFOR, armed foreigners, civilians, they could all pass through and it was only the ABiH soldiers that were stopped at ABiH-controlled checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fairly complex issue and requires an elaborate answer. If I'm to provide you with a specific answer to your question, it's very difficult for me to answer a question in a way that would satisfy you in a sufficiently precise way because I was never present at the checkpoints to observe how the MPs worked there. They were under the command of the 3rd Corps security organ, and I think it would be best to put this question to those who were involved in that field. All I have done here is express my opinion. I was never present at any of the checkpoints to observe how ABiH members performed their duties there. I had other tasks that were important and that I had to carry out. I focussed my attention on the main tasks I had to carry out. If I had been assigned the task to check how the MPs worked at the checkpoints, then I could answer your question very precisely. All I'm doing is telling you my opinion now. I'm only testifying about what I know here, and I can only tell you about my opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge or recollection, did any members of UNPROFOR or BritBat ever tell you that they had problems getting through ABiH checkpoints? Or did they ever request from you a certificate or a pass in order to get through an ABiH checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were a few such cases, but there were very few such cases. A negligible number. When my attention was drawn to a problem of that nature, I resolved the difficulty immediately. I remember an event in Busovaca in January 1993 when ABiH members, given the fight with the HVO -- well, the road in Busovaca had been completely blocked, and the international community via an UNPROFOR representative said there was a problem, that traffic couldn't pass through. They said that UNPROFOR vehicles couldn't pass through, and I went to that location. I saw the vehicle that had been positioned there by members of the ABiH, and I intervened immediately, on the spot. That checkpoint started functioning for the UNPROFOR and UNHCR vehicles and for ambulances and Red Cross vehicles. We abided by our duties in respect of international agreements and conventions. As soon as I was informed of a problem, I would try to deal with it immediately. I have said why we sometimes had serious problems or not-so-serious problems. These people weren't sufficiently trained to perform their duties. I have already mentioned the fact that we didn't have sufficiently professional officers to carry out the duties. We didn't have enough professional military policemen to carry out their duties normally. We still had to spend a lot of time in training our men. And I'm sure that well-trained men wouldn't have created any problems. They wouldn't have prevented UNPROFOR from using certain routes, certain roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever see any of these armed foreigners with young women who may have been their wives at any point in time in the first six months of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally never saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first six months of 1993, did you personally ever see any of these armed foreigners distributing food to the local population?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally never observed any such cases. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me return now, sir, to the topic of the foreigners and the problems that they caused for the 3rd Corps. You told us that following mid-April, the events in mid-April and the end of April, the 3rd Corps realised that the problem of the armed foreigners was a significant one. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We realised that they represented a problem, but it wasn't such that our attention would be detracted from our main mission. We had a main mission, a main task to carry out, but we noticed that there was a problem that concerned these foreigners and their activities in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the end of April 1993, would it be fair to say that the 3rd Corps leadership had concerns about criminal activities committed by these armed foreigners in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps command noticed that this problem was becoming increasingly complex. That's correct. The corps command tried to obtain help from the supreme command staff, help to solve the problem. I think I have mentioned the measures taken by the 3rd Corps. The 3rd Corps stepped up its activities. I've already said that the security service became more active, but this takes time. You can't have all the facts at your disposal in just one day. I don't know what sort of methods are used by these services, these operational methods that they used. They have methods that they don't speak about, they don't inform the public at large about the methods they used. And they didn't inform me about the methods they used. They performed this work as professional organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm curious, sir, because it seems to me a bit odd that if these people were causing problems and you had suspicions that they were committing crimes, that the steps to be taken included forming them into a specific unit rather than taking action to expel them or to take some other kind of military action against them. And you've explained why you didn't do that. But it just -- can you help us out in any way in terms of explaining why the solution to this problem of these armed foreigners who you were aware may have committed crimes was to put them into a unit of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you about the person who suggested that they be integrated into the 3rd Corps. Naturally, in June, they weren't 3rd Corps members. At the time, we couldn't have formed a special unit. You can't use a special unit against an unknown enemy. You don't know how many men you need in such a unit. If you believe they were the enemies of the 3rd Corps, well, I said they were a problem that appeared in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. And the 3rd Corps collected information, gathered information about them. The 3rd Corps wanted to solve the problem, but to form a special unit at the time or to confront someone, well, this is something you could have done if you had reliable information, if you could make accurate assessments, if you could assess what the consequences of an armed conflict with such a militant group would be. As for the crimes they committed, this is what we would observe in Miletici. The population said that these crimes were committed by foreigners whom they called the mujahedin. If they had said that they were army members, we would have had more reliable information because we knew who the members of the ABiH were. In such a case, we could have formed some sort of a joint, special unit to confront such a criminal group. I've also said that whenever we discovered that certain crimes had been committed, we used all the means we had available to obtain information about such events. As I have said, at the time foreigners were not members of the 3rd Corps, members of the ABiH. They certainly weren't members of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's my question, sir: Why at that point did you take steps to put them into the 3rd Corps if they weren't?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer that question if you don't understand my answer. It wasn't the 3rd Corps command's suggestion to have them join the ABiH. The 3rd Corps suggested to the supreme command staff that they should help to find a solution to the problem of foreigners. That has been my testimony before this Court. Don't put words into my mouth. I've already answered the question. I can repeat my answer if you like. I don't know how to explain this. I'm saying that the 3rd Corps didn't make this suggestion. The supreme command staff suggested that the foreigners should become part of the 3rd Corps. I don't know whether this solution was the best one that the supreme command staff could find. You should ask the supreme command staff about that, not me. I cannot say how the supreme command staff should have acted. I can't say what they should have done. That's a question I can't answer, not because I don't want to answer the question but because I quite simply can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you or, to your knowledge, did General Hadzihasanovic ever ask the supreme command staff why this step should be taken?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and I don't know what my commander General Hadzihasanovic spoke about with the supreme command staff, it wasn't for me to ask General Hadzihasanovic about his discussions with the supreme command staff, and I don't know what General Hadzihasanovic suggested to the supreme command staff. I don't know whether he suggested that the foreigners should join the 3rd Corps, but I have testified here that I had reliable information according to which General Hadzihasanovic asked the superior command to assist in solving the problem of foreigners. He said that the 3rd Corps was burdened by the problem of foreigners and that this could be a serious problem for the 3rd Corps in the future. I know that the 3rd Corps commander informed the supreme command staff of this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever personally advise the corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, that it was a bad idea to try to bring these armed foreigners into the 3rd Corps in a structured way?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember suggesting to my commander that they should become part of the 3rd Corps. As far as I can remember, I never suggested any such thing to the 3rd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir. My question is the exact opposite. Did you ever suggest or advise General Hadzihasanovic that it was a bad idea to form a unit composed of armed -- of these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having suggested any solutions. I can't remember having suggested that some sort of a unit should be formed out of those foreigners. I can't remember making such a suggestion to Commander General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, General, I'm going to turn now to a completely different topic, that being the incidents that happened in Dusina in late January 1993. Did you ever have a discussion with Colonel Robert Stewart of BritBat concerning what happened in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified that I had frequent contact with Mr. Bob Stewart. We would speak about various subjects when we met, and I can't rule out the possibility of having spoken about such a subject with Mr. Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Mr. Bob Stewart or Colonel Bob Stewart about the possibility of disciplining soldiers of the 3rd Corps for events that happened in Dusina or Lasva on the 25th or 26th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't rule out the possibility that we spoke about that subject, but I'm sure that at the time I spoke to him about what I knew with regard to the events in Dusina. I have already spoken at length about the events in Dusina. Perhaps I should say a few things in more precise terms. Perhaps I should clarify certain things. According to information I had, according to information I obtained from reports on the events in Dusina, no crimes were committed there. People were killed in fighting. People on both sides were killed in the combat. There were men from the ABiH and from the HVO who were killed in combat. So I certainly spoke about this to Bob. I couldn't have told Bob about something I knew nothing about. I spoke to Colonel Bob Stewart quite openly. I was quite frank Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond with him. So if I spoke to him about that, then I told him about the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if -- if the Croat persons who were killed in Dusina died as a result of combat-related activity, would there have been a need to discipline any soldiers or court-martial any soldiers of the ABiH for those combat-related fatalities?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, throughout my entire testimony I never said that members of the HVO were murdered. I have a very well-defined position as a soldier. I said that they were casualty in combat. My question is whether measures are taken against the soldier who shoots during combat, and this is the question that you put to me. If a soldier fires during combat, that's -- that's okay. I never said that these people were killed or murdered. They were casualty. And this is what I read in the report that I had at the time at my disposal. Later on, I received information that an investigation was carried out because the HVO claimed that a crime had been committed there, that members of the HVO were indeed killed there. And according to the information that I later had, there was an expert analysis of the fallen HVO soldiers from Dusina. I've already said that the military police at the time still were not equipped. It had been barely been established. They sought assistance from the civilian police, from their experts who had been engaged in such cases for a number of years and who had state-of-the-art equipment. The 3rd Corps did not have any equipment to establish how wound was inflicted, to carry out any forensic investigation. And this is what I have testified about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you, sir, to the 26th of January 1993 at the point in time where you were at the commission meeting, and Colonel Blaskic informed the parties that meeting about the events in Dusina. You told us about that last week. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this meeting in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the words or the information that Colonel Blaskic conveyed to you and the others who were present? What exactly did he say had happened in Dusina that day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and I cannot convey word for word what Mr. Tihomir Blaskic said at the time; however, the essence of what he said was that the Croats in Dusina had been killed, that the BiH army had committed a crime there, that they had murdered Croats there in that area. I believe this is what Mr. Tihomir Blaskic said, as far as I can remember as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, do you recall approximately what time you left that meeting on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time. I can give you an approximate time. It was sometime in the afternoon. I only remember one detail. The UNPROFOR representatives wanted to go back while it was still daylight, and they insisted on that because of the combat operations in Busovaca. It was very risky to pass through that area during the night. I remember that the meeting ended sometime in the afternoon. I don't know when. I believe that it was around 1500 hours or maybe even 1600 hours; that is, 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon. However, I can't remember exactly when the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us, sir, that you returned or you were taken by UNPROFOR to the 3rd Corps command in Zenica, and you passed this information on to the commander, General Hadzihasanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And this is what I've said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any steps you took after you returned to the 3rd Corps headquarters to try to determine what had happened in Dusina on that day? What did you do that late afternoon, early evening?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, in the afternoon I couldn't do anything because I was on my way back to Zenica. However, if you insist that I should tell you what happened from the moment when I reported to General Hadzihasanovic and when I briefed him of what I had heard and of the conclusions of that meeting on the 26th in Kiseljak, I can tell you that after that I took reports that had arrived by then at the command of the 3rd Corps. And from the reports, I learned that there had been combat operations and that there were casualties on both sides. Those were the initial reports that had arrived at the 3rd Corps command. These reports described things differently to what Blaskic claimed at the meeting on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to please take a look at the bundle in front of you. And if you could look at the document numbered P251. Sir, would this be one of the reports that had arrived late in the day on the 26th of January 1993 and to which you just referred that you would have taken a look at?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having seen this report. I did not have an opportunity to look at this report. This report is addressed to the regional defence staff of Zenica. I didn't go to the regional staff of Zenica. I went to the 3rd Corps command. The headquarters of the regional staff was not the same place as the headquarters of the 3rd Corps. I only looked at the reports that had arrived at the command of the 3rd Corps. I didn't go to any of the subordinate units to collect reports that had reached them, and therefore I could not read those reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then ask you this question: You told us that on the morning of the 27th, you returned to Kiseljak for a meeting of the Kiseljak joint commission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what time was that meeting, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the meeting that took place on the 27th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was in the morning, or maybe sometime around noon. In any case, it was not early in the morning. It was either in the late morning hours or around noon. I can't tell you with morning hours or around noon. I can't tell you with any precision whether it was at 10.00 or 11.00 or sometime between 10.00 and 11.00. In any case, it was closer to noon than to the early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note for the transcript that on page 24, line 17, after the word "indeed," beginning with "this meeting was in the morning," was actually the witness's answer and was not part of the question I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at this meeting on the 27th of January 1993, can you tell us to the best of your recollection what you reported at that meeting concerning the events in Dusina the preceding day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I reported that there had been fighting in Dusina between the HVO and the BiH Army. I also said that there had been casualties on both sides, and that was the essence of my report at that meeting on the 27th in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 26th of January 1993 or in the following few days, did you become aware of the fact that five or six HVO soldiers had been captured in Dusina on the 26th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Were you aware that Serif Patkovic was involved in the events in Dusina on January 26th 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that members of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were present in Dusina on 26 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, members of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade were in the area of Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, do you know in January 1993 who was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can remember well, it was Mr. Serif Patkovic. He was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever discuss with Serif Patkovic or question him Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond about the events that occurred in Dusina on the 26th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did not discuss Dusina with Mr. Patkovic. I did not ask Serif Patkovic anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if anyone from the 3rd Corps security services or military police discussed the events in Dusina on the 26th of January 1993 with Mr. Patkovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that later, Mr. Patkovic was promoted and received awards, including a Golden Lily?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Mr. Serif Patkovic received a Golden Lily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know an individual by the name of Vehid Subotic who also went by the nickname "Geler"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know this person, and I've never had an opportunity to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or did you ever read any documents indicating that anyone from the 3rd Corps security service or military police spoke to Mr. Subotic, also known as Geler? Do you ever see any reports or documents that any one spoke with him about events in Dusina on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never read the security services report about Dusina. And I never saw anybody named Subotic mentioned in any of these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of any such security service reports concerning the events of Dusina, 26 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that the services of the 3rd Corps were involved in the issue of Dusina because an investigation was being carried out, together with the civilian police in order to establish what had happened. I had that information. However, I never read the report of the security services on that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you told us earlier that Dusina was a significant event because it was the first time the ABiH had been accused of committing war crimes by the HVO. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that this was the first time that the HVO accused the BiH Army of having committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yet, sir, you never read the report of the security service on this incident to inform yourself so that if this topic came up at following meetings you could explain to the HVO and the international representatives what the conclusions of that report were?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified before this Court that I read the reports that had arrived in the 3rd Corps covering the events in Dusina and the Dusina-related reports. After that, I never read the Dusina-related reports because as far as I know, this was done together with the municipal defence staff. As far as I know, a joint commission was established there that took over the fallen soldiers of the HVO from the hospital in Zenica. I had that information. However, I never read the report drafted by the security service or that commission that had handed over the fallen HVO soldiers from Dusina. I did not have an occasion to read the hospital postmortem report. I had information that this had been done officially. I don't know what expert methods were used to do that. I only know that these people had been murdered, killed -- actually that they fell in combat, and that there was a report of the commission that worked in that area; however, I never read that report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: You went to Dusina. You've told us about going to Dusina with Mr. Nakic, and I believe you said Mr. Fleming. And you told us that you spoke to a few people in Dusina and the immediate vicinity of Dusina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke to the local commander in Dusina. I can't remember his name. I don't know what his name was. But I said that he was the local commander. I remember that. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I told you his name was Hazim Barucija, would that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the name. It was a long time ago. I can't even ever asking his name. I don't know this man's name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you tell us to the best of your recollection what questions you asked this local commander and what information he conveyed to you about the events that occurred in Dusina on 26 January 1993. And I would ask you, if it's possible, to be as specific as you can about what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Franjo Nakic was present during that exchange. When I asked him what had happened in Dusina, he replied that there had been fighting in Dusina, that there had been combat operations and that there were casualties on both sides. This is -- as far as I can remember this is what this local commander told us when we met with him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember asking this local commander or whether he volunteered information that there was a small number of HVO soldiers who had been captured that day? Did you ask him about any prisoners that may have been taken?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I asked this local commander if there were any HVO prisoners. I also don't remember him volunteering that information. I can't remember that. I've told you what I can remember. I've told you what I remember. I remember that this commander answered my question, and my question was what happened in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me turn very quickly and ask you one or two questions about Maline prior to the break. Did you receive any information concerning the events that took place in Maline on the 8th of June 1993 that in any way suggested to you that the armed foreigners were involved in criminal activity on that day in Maline Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But prior to that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you issue an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that point, you had no information about the involvement of armed foreigners in Bikosi on the 8th of June 1993, just so that we're absolutely clear on that. Would that be the case.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that the first time I learned the correct information, I had information that there was a suspicion about civilians having been killed, and I've told you that I received that information from the European monitors and that at the beginning of August 1993, we went to the site. The European monitors headed by Mr. Remy and Father Radic was also a member of that delegation. And I also told you that we were taken to the location by a soldier who showed us the place where two graves were, where the bodies of all those who fell in combat in that area had been buried. I also testified about a report that I sent to the supreme command staff describing the events that had happened in the village of Miletici. This was at the request of international institutions. I remember also that I've testified about sending this request to the subordinate command and that we received a report, and based on this report, I drafted my report for the supreme command describing what had happened in Maline. This is what I have already testified about. However, the first time I learned about the crime having been committed by foreigners was during the Kordic case while I testified in that case. This is what I knew about the event, and this is how I have testified so Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. You should inform the Chamber that during this last session, I was informed via email from the Registrar who apparently conferred with the Chamber's legal officer, and in fact my time has now expired. I note that at one point, my learned colleague for General Hadzihasanovic asked for additional time and was denied that. And so as a matter of fairness and principle, we will finish our cross-examination at this point in time, having taken the same amount of time as the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic. And just as it was the situation with my learned colleague, we would have had additional questions, but we're well aware of time constraints, and I certainly don't want to be in a position of taking significantly longer than the Defence did on their direct examination. Thank you. That concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's 25 to 11.00. We'll have our break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume, and I will give the floor to Defence counsel for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General Merdan.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'll now put some questions that were put to you or that have to do with questions put my learned colleague in the course of their cross-examination. My first question has to do with the question that was put to you yesterday, a question that had to do with your testimony in the Kordic case with regard to the identity of the first commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Do you remember that question, and do you remember the answers you provided?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, at the time, you said that there had been a significant error, and you said that that was possible since you were being asked to remind -- remember something, so was this your answer with regard to the testimony in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, in the course of your testimony before this Trial Chamber, you said -- or you testified up until quarter to 2.00. And when answering these questions, you said that you were feeling tired. At the time yesterday, did you feel tired given the length that the examination had taken?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, I was feeling very tired. In the afternoon, I asked for medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if I said that yesterday -- according to the transcript, your testimony came to an end at page 70, and the questions in the Kordic case referred to by the Prosecution yesterday were referred to or were noted on page 12.909 and 12.910, and this was on page 92 of the transcript. As a result, this means that you were answering these questions after having been examined for about five or six hours. Can you remember when in the course of your examination you were asked about the 7th Muslim Brigade? Was it at the beginning of your testimony or at the end of your testimony on that day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the testimony in the Kordic case. The testimony was very difficult, which is the case here, too. I remember that that was on the second day of my testimony, and it was towards the end of my testimony at which point I was really very tired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the part of the transcript my learned colleague referred to when talking about the witness's testimony. We have a sufficient number of copies for the Chamber and my learned colleagues. And I just have one other question to put to the witness -- a few more questions to put to the witness in relation to this subject. The testimony that was given in the Kordic case on the 25th of January -- well, I have taken just the first page from that testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you, Mr. President. I'm wondering if perhaps my learned colleague can explain to us how it might be helpful showing the witness these pages in light of his previous testimony that he doesn't understand English. And I would also ask that she not be permitted to lead the witness during her re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as the document in English is concerned, the witness said that he didn't understand English. What would the purpose be of showing the witness a document that is English? The answers and questions are in English? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like everyone in the courtroom to be aware of the fact that I will be showing the witness the part of this transcript in the same way that my colleague proceeded when he asked the witness questions. Because the witness mentioned the fact that he was tired, and he mentioned the possibility of an error when answering the questions put to him by the Prosecution. So this is why I would like to read part of this transcript, and this will be interpreted to the witness in his own language. I will then ask the witness a question that relates to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what would you say about the objection to asking the witness leading questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll do my best, and I know that I shouldn't ask the witness leading questions. If I do ask a leading question and my colleague objects to it, I'll try to rephrase the question. When I put questions to witnesses in my own language, I try to avoid putting leading questions. That's my duty, and I will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on page 12.909 in this transcript, in line 9, the following was stated: "Well, that was precisely my question. Would you agree with me that the 7th Muslim Brigade was under the command of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that we should add a dash, as you say." Your answer: "Not really any -- what I'm saying is that the 7th Muslim Brigade was under the command of the 3rd Corps's command." Question: "Right. So if we are talking about the chain of command and who makes part of the 3rd Corps, you will agree with me that the special unit, El Mujahed, was also under the 3rd Corps's command, and it numbered about a thousand men?" Answer: "Yes, that is true. But will you give me the time frame because we may be referring to different period of time. I say it was under the 3rd Corps's command, but again, it depends on the period of time." Question: "I'm referring to the time when Asim Koricic commanded the 7th Muslim Brigade, so that would be the brigade was founded on the 1st of December 1992. So that would be that period until sometime in the summer 1993." Answer: "I believe you made a mistake because Asim Koricic was never a commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade. And the El Mujahed was founded as far as I know in late 1993 or perhaps early 1994. And when it was established it was placed under the command of the 3rd Corps's command." General, are these the answers that you provided in the Kordic case at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember providing these answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we can see there are two units referred to in the questions. Which units are they?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's the 7th Muslim Brigade and the El mujahedin detachment that were referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given what you have confirmed both yesterday and today, given the fact that you confirmed that after having been examined for a certain Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond period of time you become tired, would you say that the error that you noticed yesterday might have anything to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Leading. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you provide me with an additional explanation of the reason for the error you made at the time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, before this Trial Chamber, I tried to explain the reason for which I made such an error. That was quite obviously a slip that I made. I would never have made such a noticeable error. I said that I was very tired and that it's quite possible that when questions are put to me, the time period must be very specific. There were many things that happened in the 3rd Corps in a very short period of time. And this requires a lot of concentration on my part during the entire period of my testimony. It's possible that I made a mistake. I've already made a few mistakes. I made a few mistakes when testifying before this Chamber last week. But when I notice an error, I would like to ask the Chamber to understand the error. I apologise for such errors. When I notice an error, I try to explain the reasons for which I made an error. I never intentionally committed an error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was Asim Koricic ever the El mujahedin commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Asim Koricic was never the commander of the El mujahedin detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in 1993 or in the year 2000 or in the course of your testimony, this testimony, at any point in time did you have any reason not to say who the commander of a certain brigade was, for example, of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason for me not to say everything that I am aware of, and I will inform the Chamber of everything I know. This is my duty. And I'm attempting to inform the Chamber of everything I know and of everything that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, thank you. At the beginning of the cross-examination, my learned colleague put a number of questions to you that relate to this map. I would like to ask you to approach the map again so that I can ask you some questions that relate to that part of the cross-examination. You said that at the bottom of the map, it says "Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic," but that there was no signature. That's what you said in response to questions put to you by my learned colleague. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't hear you now either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness could use this device here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were shown this map, you told us that this is the commander's working map, and you saw that it was not signed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When does a working map become the commander's real working map? Does it have anything to do with the fact that you noticed that the map isn't signed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, I believe, and I know, that every document becomes valid once it is signed. The commander's working map can be used only by the commander or by a person designated by him to enter things on to the map. Once the map is signed, it becomes the ownership of the person who signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in the 3rd Corps, was there only one map, or were there several maps in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps, and I know that in other similar armies in the world, there are several maps at the level of corps commands. The same case was in the 3rd Corps. There were several maps of this sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of these maps is the most detailed one? Which one is the one where most details are entered depicting the situation in the corps itself?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know as a military professional, most of the details are entered into the map of the operations centre of the 3rd Corps. The operations centre of the 3rd Corps is part of the 3rd Corps staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the commander needs certain tactical details on everyday events, who would it be to provide those details to the commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These details would be provided by the operations centre because all the information on the events taking place in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps is collected by the operations centre. And then this information is forwarded to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in response to my learned friend's question, you've told us that this map provides main information about the enemy forces and the commands of operations groups and brigades. In addition to the difference in terms of the number of details, are there any other differences between the operations centre map and the map which is in the commander's office and serves as his working map?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are major differences between these two maps. The operations centre map contains all the information on everything that is happening in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, in all the regions, in all the fields. The corps commander on the other hand enters on his map only what he deems important for him. The corps commander has to think operatively. He has to look at what might happen in the future, what might occur during the exercise of his main mission. I've already testified to great length about that. The main mission was the defence of the territory from the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember, and I will remind you, on page 7, lines 9 to 14, the Prosecutor asked you whether these lines mean that there was combat going on in that area. When you were looking at the area without dotted lines, in the same answer you said that maybe there was combat there, but at a lower level, at battalion and brigade levels, at a lower tactical level. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember talking about that and why there are no dotted lines in this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, given your military experience and the fact that you were deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, and when you're looking at this from the military aspect, why would the commander be interested in following combat at a lower tactical lower, for example, combat where a company would be engaged? Would that be his main task? If not, would he still sometimes wish to be involved and follow such combat?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My military experience, and especially my work with the commander, Mr. -- General Enver Hadzihasanovic tells me that the commander of the 3rd Corps took more interest in operative matters. However, every combat may be of significance for a corps commander. You may not exclude the importance of any one combat operation. It may happen that a combat operation of a lower tactical level does merit interest of the commander of the corps. For example, if such a combat may have operational consequences, even if it is at a lower level, if such a combat at a lower level might have operational consequences, then at any given moment, the commander may pay some attention to such combat. However, in principle, the corps commander will pay more attention to the combat of operational and strategic interest. That is the main task of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already explained which units took part in the combat in Dusina. Given the lower level of units which were involved in combat there, did the corps commander show any interest -- should he have shown any interest in that combat given its tactical importance?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my experience and my knowledge, my war experience and knowing my commander, and I believe that I knew my commander rather well, I can say that the combat operation in Dusina was of tactical Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond significance. However, one has to bear in mind that there is a very important facility in the vicinity of Dusina. This is the Lasva junction. The Lasva junction was always of major significance for the corps commander. It had operational significance, and if there's any combat taking place in the vicinity of such a facility which has operational significance, every commander should pay a lot of attention to the combat of tactical significance in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My learned friend asked you about the strength of the 3rd Corps, and you said that the corps had between twenty-five and thirty thousand troops. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I answered that question. I could not provide precise information because it was a long time ago. And also, the strength of the corps changed rather quickly. We had a lot of casualties. We replenished the units of the 3rd Corps on a day-to-day basis. At any given time, I had between 25.000 and 30.000 troops, and that includes both officers and foot soldiers. Yes, I did mention the figure of twenty-five to thirty thousand troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in order to assess the strength of a military unit, is it only the number of troops that would be relevant, or are there any other factors that have to be taken into account when answering that question?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strength of any unit including the 3rd Corps is determined based on a number of factors. I've already mentioned one factor. That is the number of troops. This factor is important. I cannot say it is the most important factor, but it is very important. The next factor which is very important is the armament of that unit. Here I'm referring to the number of weapons and the type of weapons that that unit or the 3rd Corps has. The next factor is the communication and the roads in the area of responsibility. The next one would be the logistical support, the strength of the enemy also has an impact on the strength of a unit which includes the 3rd Corps as well. In other words, there are a number of different factors which may impact the strength of a unit. I could talk for a long time about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to the number of troops, in the course of your testimony so far, you have mentioned the level of equipment and the lack of arms. So I won't go into that again. You have now mentioned the strength of the enemy. Can you show us on this map where the Serbian forces were and where were the forces of the 3rd Corps facing the Serbian aggressor? Can you tell us how many defence lines facing the Serbian enemy you had and how long was the defence line during the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to deploy one's own forces facing the enemy, and you are asking me only about the aggressor forces, one has to have intelligence. According to our intelligence, there were three aggressor corps attacking the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. The most important area was the area to the west of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps where we had the 1st Krajina Corps. I've already testified before this Court that the Serbian aggressor towards the end of 1992 had a lot of success in the area from Jajce towards Travnik. There were major operations being carried out there. The 2nd Corps of the aggressor was deployed in the area of Maglaj, around Zavidovici. Some of our troops were engaged in the -- in lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. This is where the 3rd Krajina Corps was involved. So we had three aggressor corps which were attacking the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. And when you look at the line that the 3rd Corps was defending, I'll try to draw a line. Here was a small area where we had contact with the HVO and where the HVO was in contact with the aggressor. The rest of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps was huge. Some of our troops were engaged in lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. So the line here was very long if you look at it as a single line, and this is where all of our defence troops were deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you have not answered my question. How long was that line approximately? If I put it to you that in the Blaskic case, the Prosecution mentioned the figure of 500 kilometres, would that correspond to the length of line that you have in mind facing the Serbian enemy?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the transcript of my testimony last week and the beginning of this week, I said at one point that the line facing the aggressor was approximately 500 kilometres, which confirms the figure that you put to me. I can't give you the precise measurements. If you were to measure the line precisely, it would be about 500 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of the total number of troops and out of your total equipment, how much did you have to engage on a daily basis in order to defend the territory from further advance of the Serbian aggressor?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We engaged most of our strength, the strength of the 3rd Corps, in order to defend such a long line. According to my estimate, our daily engagement was at least two-thirds of the available troops of the 3rd Corps. About 80 per cent of our troops were engaged on the defence lines facing the aggressor against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you giving us the main factors that determine the strength of a unit, including the 3rd Corps, you also mentioned the mobility of troops. I believe that this was what you said a little while ago, if I am correct. Tell me, what was the mobility in the area of the 3rd Corps of the BiH Army units? And what was the mobility of the enemy units at the time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that there was a huge difference there. I've already said that one of the elements that determined the strength of a unit is its mobility, the mobility of that unit. If you look at the entire territory of the 3rd Corps, you can see immediately, and I knew it in practice, and I witnessed all of these events, you can see immediately that the mobility of the 3rd Corps units was very low, that the roads were not passable. Very often, we had to drive our logistical support to the defence lines, to our troops on the defence lines. Unlike the Serbian aggressor who had a huge manoeuvre area, they had roads, they had communications, they enjoyed support from Yugoslavia, from the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. Likewise, I can say that the units of the HVO also had good roads, especially the roads towards the Republic of Croatia. The roads there were very good. If you look at the area where the troops of the HVO were engaged in Central Bosnia, you will see that there are -- there were no BiH units there that would prevent them from moving around. So the HVO could deploy their troops very quickly. They had very good transportation means that helped them with that. We couldn't do that, and it was a major problem for the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if I have understood you correctly, the Republika Srpska forces, just like the HVO, in addition to having such mobility, could also rely for logistics on Yugoslavia, and the other forces could rely on Croatia. Tell me, in 1993, could the army be provided with the weapons and the equipment that they needed to mount a defence on either side?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact that there was an embargo on the delivery of weapons to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when you examine the situation in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, the 3rd Corps was practically completely encircled, either by the Serbian aggressor or by the HVO.
